en: Deno has this built-in permissions concept,
and that's a key difference to Node, in case
you know Node.
In Node.js, you can execute any script just
like this, and Node will not ask for
permissions. So any script is allowed to do
anything in the end.
That's different in Deno.
By default,
Deno scripts may not read files, write
files,
or use environment variables, or interact
with the network.
And there are a couple of other things too,
but these are the most important things
which are not allowed by default.
Now that's a great security mechanism, but
sometimes
you want to write a file.
For example, here in our code, we want to
run this code. We don't want it to crash.
Well, no worries. Of course, you can still
do these things with Deno. You just have to
assign the right permissions to your script
execution explicitly.
And for example, for reading files, that's
done by adding
the --allow-read flag to your Deno run
command. For writing, it's --allow-write.
It's --allow-env for accessing environment
variables. And it's --allow-net for
interacting with the network.
There also are variations in case you don't
wanna allow reading all files but you wanna
restrict it to certain files. You can, for
example, also pass the path to the file
which should be allowed to allow-read. The
same for writing. You can make clear which
environment variables should be accessible,
and you can, for example, also lock down
network access to specific domains.
So it's not an either nothing or everything
decision, it's a very granular decision
where you can really fine-tune this to your
needs.
So
if I go back here,
in order to run our code, we need to run
deno run
and then
--allow-write
to allow writing to all files,
or
If we wanna just allow writing to test.txt,
allowWrite equals test.txt
and then your script file name, so
deno-core.ts.
And now this compiles and eventually is
done. And as you see, it created the
test.txt file
with the message we specified in our code.
So that is how Deno works in general and how
you deal with its permissions. But not just
that, now you also saw some of the core APIs
in action.
You saw setTimeout, which is available in
Deno, and this global Deno object,
which my IDE doesn't recognize right now,
but which is available,
as you can clearly tell by the fact that the
script executed successfully.
And this global Deno object gives us access
to all these core APIs which essentially
contain all you might need to build any kind
of application. In this case, a very simple
application that writes to a file and
creates the file if it doesn't exist yet.
